channel.title: Formal Political Economy (Edenhofer, Trinity 2026)
channel.description: Weekly audio companion to Jacob Edenhofer's Trinity Term 2026 course at Nuffield College, Oxford. One episode per week, working through that week's canonical model and the literature around it: electoral accountability, party competition and pork barrel, electoral rules, interest groups and lobbying, and democratic backsliding.
channel.itunes:subtitle: A second introduction to formal political economy
channel.itunes:author: Reed Schwartz

item.title: M01 — Models of Electoral Accountability
item.itunes:title: M01 — Models of Electoral Accountability
item.description:
Week 1 — Models of Electoral Accountability (27 April – 1 May)

Whether elections discipline politicians by selecting good types or by sanctioning bad performance — and why the distinction collapses once the two mechanisms interact.

Readings

  • Ashworth, Bueno de Mesquita & Friedenberg (2017), Accountability and Information in Elections — AEJ: Micro
  • Maskin & Tirole (2004), The Politician and the Judge — AER
  • Besley & Prat (2006), Handcuffs for the Grabbing Hand — AER
  • Stokes (2005), Perverse Accountability — APSR
  • Duggan & Martinelli (2017), The Political Economy of Dynamic Elections — JEL
  • Canes-Wrone, Herron & Shotts (2001), Leadership and Pandering — AJPS
  • Fox & Shotts (2009), Delegates or Trustees? — JOP
  • Landa & Duell (2015), Social Identity and Electoral Accountability — AJPS
  • Dynes & Holbein (2020), Noisy Retrospection — APSR

The week's sharpest result is that more information can make accountability worse: when effort and ability are substitutes, harder work by an incumbent muddies the signal voters use to judge type. Stokes and Besley & Prat both describe accountability running backwards — machine monitoring in one, media capture in the other. Dynes & Holbein sit awkwardly against all of it: if party control barely moves policy outcomes, what exactly are voters sanctioning?

Not covered: Persson & Tabellini ch. 4.4/9.2–9.3, Fearon (1999) and Lupia & McCubbins (1998) are books and not in the source set.

item.title: M02 — Party Competition and Pork-Barrel Politics
item.itunes:title: M02 — Party Competition and Pork-Barrel Politics
item.description:
Week 2 — Party Competition and Pork-Barrel Politics (4–8 May)

How Downsian convergence breaks once you add valence, probabilistic voting and the ability to target transfers — and what a party actually is in a formal model.

Readings

  • Dixit & Londregan (1996), The Determinants of Success of Special Interests in Redistributive Politics — JOP
  • Dixit & Londregan (1998), Ideology, Tactics, and Efficiency in Redistributive Politics — QJE
  • Shepsle & Weingast (1981), Political Preferences for the Pork Barrel — AJPS
  • Snyder & Ting (2002), An Informational Rationale for Political Parties — AJPS
  • Caillaud & Tirole (2002), Parties as Political Intermediaries — QJE
  • Aldrich (1983), A Downsian Spatial Model with Party Activism — APSR
  • Strøm (1990), A Behavioral Theory of Competitive Political Parties — AJPS

The swing-versus-core question turns on how efficiently parties can target, not on ideology. Snyder & Ting, Caillaud & Tirole and Aldrich give three incompatible answers to what a party solves — an informational problem, an intermediation problem, or activist aggregation. Shepsle & Weingast's pork result is legislative-organisational and sits at an angle to all of them.

Not covered: Adams/Merrill/Grofman chs. 1–3 and the Cox (2010) chapter are books and not in the source set.

item.title: M03 — Formal Models of Electoral Rules
item.itunes:title: M03 — Formal Models of Electoral Rules
item.description:
Week 3 — Formal Models of Electoral Rules (11–15 May)

Why majoritarian systems produce narrowly targeted spending and PR systems produce broad programmes — and whether that regularity comes from targetability or from coalition formation.

Readings

  • Persson, Roland & Tabellini (2000), Comparative Politics and Public Finance — JPE
  • Myerson (1993), Incentives to Cultivate Favored Minorities — APSR
  • Lizzeri & Persico (2005), A Drawback of Electoral Competition — JEEA
  • Iversen & Soskice (2006), Electoral Institutions and the Politics of Coalitions — APSR
  • Austen-Smith (2000), Redistributing Income under Proportional Representation — JPE
  • Ashworth & Bueno de Mesquita (2006), Delivering the Goods — JOP
  • Callander (2005), Duverger's Hypothesis, the Run-Off Rule, and Electoral Competition — Political Analysis
  • Becher (2016), Endogenous Credible Commitment — AJPS

Persson–Roland–Tabellini and Iversen–Soskice explain the same cross-national fiscal pattern with different machinery, and the episode's central question is what evidence could tell them apart.

Not covered: the required reading for this week is Persson & Tabellini ch. 9, a book chapter not in the source set — the episode is carried entirely by the optional articles.

item.title: M04 — Interest Groups and Lobbying
item.itunes:title: M04 — Interest Groups and Lobbying
item.description:
Week 4 — Interest Groups and Lobbying (18–22 May)

What lobbying actually buys: policy, access, or the legislative labour of allies already on your side.

Readings

  • Schnakenberg & Turner (2024), Formal Theories of Special Interest Influence — ARPS (SocArXiv preprint)
  • Awad (2024), Understanding Influence in Informational Lobbying — Interest Groups & Advocacy (SocArXiv preprint)
  • Grossman & Helpman (1994), Protection for Sale — AER
  • Hall & Deardorff (2006), Lobbying as Legislative Subsidy — APSR
  • Laffont & Tirole (1991), A Theory of Regulatory Capture — QJE
  • Ansolabehere, de Figueiredo & Snyder (2003), Why Is There so Little Money in U.S. Politics? — JEP
  • Bertrand, Bombardini & Trebbi (2014), Is It Whom You Know or What You Know? — AER
  • Wolton (2021), Lobbying, Inside and Out — QJPS (LSE working paper version)
  • Hirsch, Kang, Montagnes & You (2023), Lobbyists as Gatekeepers — JOP (author copy)
  • Besley & Coate (2001), Lobbying and Welfare in a Representative Democracy — RESTUD
  • Zingales (2017), Towards a Political Theory of the Firm — JEP
  • You (2017), Ex Post Lobbying — JOP
  • Kim (2017), Political Cleavages within Industry — APSR

The standing puzzle: if Protection for Sale is right about the returns, observed lobbying spending is orders of magnitude too small.

Not covered: Culpepper, Quiet Politics and Business Power, is a book and not in the source set.

item.title: M05 — Democratic Backsliding
item.itunes:title: M05 — Democratic Backsliding
item.description:
Week 5 — Democratic Backsliding (25–29 May)

Why voters would rationally hand power to leaders who dismantle the constraints protecting them.

Readings

  • Grillo, Luo, Nalepa & Prato (2024), Theories of Democratic Backsliding — ARPS
  • Gratton & Lee (2024), Liberty, Security, and Accountability — RESTUD
  • Luo & Przeworski (2023), Democracy and Its Vulnerabilities — QJPS (author working-paper draft)
  • Acemoglu, Robinson & Torvik (2013), Why Do Voters Dismantle Checks and Balances? — RESTUD
  • Bernhardt, Krasa & Shadmehr (2022), Demagogues and the Economic Fragility of Democracies — AER
  • Graham & Svolik (2020), Democracy in America? — APSR
  • Helmke, Kroeger & Paine (2022), Democracy by Deterrence — AJPS
  • Weingast (1997), The Political Foundations of Democracy and the Rule of Law — APSR
  • Kaufman & Haggard (2019), Democratic Decline in the United States — Perspectives on Politics

Three competing engines: a liberty–security tradeoff, incumbent entrenchment dynamics, and voters trading democratic principle for partisan advantage. Weingast's coordination account and Helmke et al.'s deterrence model may be the same mechanism in different vocabulary.
